examples: Which book is the most interesting?
How long does it take from here?
fields.explain:
Remember that どの is always followed by a noun; if there is none, switch to どれ.
To ask about a person politely: use どの方 instead of どの人.
To ask about degree: どのくらい/どのぐらい goes with V/A/名詞+です.
For origin/affiliation, どこのN is very natural in conversation: どこの会社ですか.

“どの + N” asks you to identify one specific noun among several options: “Which …?”.
“どのくらい/どのぐらい” asks about degree, time, or quantity: “how much/how long”.
It cannot stand alone; if there is no noun, use どれ (which one).
For origin/affiliation, どこのN is usually more natural: どこの国／どこの会社.
fields.notes:
“どのくらい” ≈ “どれくらい” (both are common; どれくらい is slightly more colloquial).
For a specific point in time, use “何時／何分／何日” instead of どの.
“どの辺” is casual; the more polite form is “どのあたりですか”.
mistakes: Using どの alone: ×どのが好き？ → ✓ どれが好き？ or ✓ どの映画が好き？
Confusing どの with どこの when asking about origin: ✓ どこの国／会社.
Forgetting the noun after どの, which leaves information missing in JLPT answers.
Confusing どのくらい (degree) with いくつ/いくら (quantity/price). Choose correctly based on the meaning of the question.

rows: どれがあなたのですか。
どこの<ruby>会社<rt>かいしゃ</rt></ruby>ですか。
どのくらい<ruby>時間<rt>じかん</rt></ruby>が<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>？

fields.meaning: Which one（pronoun; distinguish from どの + N — see the どの～ entry）
fields.connection: どれ + (です/particle)（stands alone, not followed by N）
examples: Apples, mandarin oranges, and bananas — which will you buy?

A: Which umbrella is yours?
B: The red one.
fields.explain:
Identifies one item within a group of three or more.

どれ : which one
どのN : which N

examples: Please choose any one of these.
All the colors are the same price.
I'd be happy with any of the presents.
fields.explain:
Friendly; often used when letting someone else choose: “どれでもいいです”.
Natural in instructions/price lists: “どれでも同じ価格”.
“どれでも” is not used to modify a noun directly; change it to “どのNでも”.
If there is no clear list, consider using なんでも (anything at all) instead of どれでも.

“どれでも” expresses no distinction among options that already exist: “any of them is fine”.
Often used with いい／大丈夫／構いません to show agreement/no specific requirement.
When you need to modify a noun, use “どのNでも” instead of “どれでもN”.
The scope of “どれでも” must be a finite set of options that is visible or listed.
fields.notes:
In service settings, “どれでもどうぞ” is a polite way of inviting free choice.
“どれでも +同じ” is common in promotions and combo deals.
With verbs that ask you to choose one, どれでも emphasizes “not being picky”; どれも (affirmative) emphasizes “all are ...” (a different nuance).
mistakes: ×どれでも席→ ✓どの席でも（modifying a noun requires どのNでも）
Wrong scope: to say “anything at all” in general, use なんでも, not どれでも.
Confusing it with negative どれも: “どれも〜ません” = “none of them”, completely different from “どれでも”.
Using どれでも for places/times: use どこでも／いつでも respectively.

rows: Any one of them is fine
どれも<ruby>好<rt>す</rt></ruby>きです／どれも<ruby>好<rt>す</rt></ruby>きではありません。
Not limited to a specific list
どこでもいい／いつでも<ruby>大丈夫<rt>だいじょうぶ</rt></ruby>。

examples: Shall I help you with anything?
Why don't we have something to drink together?
fields.explain:
Expresses indefiniteness, keeping politeness and distance: it avoids pointing directly at “a specific X”.
In questions,何か implies an expectation that the answer is “yes”:何か問題がありますか。
を after何か is often dropped in conversation:何か食べる？ (casual).
Used with 〜ませんか to make a gentle invitation/suggestion.
For total negation, use何も～ません, not何か～ません.

何か expresses an unspecified “something”.
Often used in affirmative sentences, exploratory questions, and invitations/suggestions to stay vague and polite.
With あります/います it expresses “there is something” (an object/person/animal) without specifying what.
何か is not used with the negative form to say “not … anything” (use何も～ません in that case).
In negative questions with 〜ませんか,何か softens the sentence: “Shall we …?”
fields.notes:
“何かありますか” can mean “Did something happen?” depending on the context (not only “Is there anything?”).
“何か＋Nを＋ください” is more polite than “何かください” when you have a kind of thing in mind:何か飲み物をください。
Negative questions with 〜ませんか and何か often carry a nuance of invitation:何か食べませんか（＝let's eat something together）.
In spoken language,何か is sometimes shortened to “なんか” (colloquial), but on the exam you should keep何か.
mistakes: Using何か with a negative to say “not … anything”: ×何か食べません → correct:何も食べません。
Not dropping を is not wrong in spoken language, but in JLPT written language you should be standard:何かを食べます（acceptable),何か食べます（more natural).
Confusing何か and何:
何を飲みますか（what will you drink? a specific question）
何か飲みますか（will you drink anything? a suggestion).
Misreading何かありますか as “is there a specific X?”; it actually asks in general “is there anything (any matter)?”.

rows: どれか<ruby>選<rt>えら</rt></ruby>んでください。

examples: On my days off, I don't do anything.
I don't know anything about what happened yesterday.
fields.explain:
Emphasizes “not a single thing/doing nothing at all” → a firm, total nuance.
を after何も is usually dropped:何も食べません（more natural than何もを食べません）.
In casual style, use ない:何もない／何もしない。
For general negation of existence,何もありません（there is nothing at all） is very common in announcements/polite answers.

何も～ません/ない is a total negation pattern: “not … anything at all”, “nothing”.
Always used with a verb/adjective in the negative form; not used with the affirmative.
Used with あります/います to say “there is nothing (at all)”.
The degree can be emphasized with supporting words (N4 and above) such as全然/全く; at N5,何も + Vません alone is enough.
fields.notes:
“何もない” can stand alone as a complete sentence:何もない（There is nothing at all）.
“何も問題はありません” is grammatically correct:何も＋N＋は＋ありません → “There is no problem at all”.
In a polite answer, you can say: いいえ、何もありません。
With verbs of cognition,何も覚えていません／何も聞いていません are both natural.
mistakes: Using it with the affirmative: ×何もあります → incorrect. Use the negative:何もありません。
Adding を after何も: ×何もを食べません → を is usually dropped:何も食べません。
Confusing it with何か:
何か食べます（eat something, affirmative)
何も食べません（not eat anything, negative).
Using いません for inanimate objects (×何もいません for objects in a room) → the correct form is何もありません.

rows: Must be used with the negative
どれも<ruby>好<rt>す</rt></ruby>きじゃない。
<ruby>全然<rt>ぜんぜん</rt></ruby><ruby>分<rt>わ</rt></ruby>かりません。

examples: If you have any questions, feel free to ask anything.
fields.explain:
なんでも is used to speak generally, without limiting the options. It suits both polite and casual speech.
なんでもいい shows “not being picky”; add です to be more polite: なんでもいいです。
なんでもない is used to reassure someone or to downplay importance: “it's nothing/it's fine”.
Avoid using なんでも with a ない-type negative to say “not … anything”; use 何も…ない for that meaning.

なんでも expresses an all-inclusive scope: “anything …”, “whatever it is …”. Usually used with affirmative verbs/ adjectives.
なんでもいい: “anything is fine”, showing there is no specific requirement.
なんでもない: a set phrase meaning “it's nothing/it's fine”, not to be understood as “everything is not” (different from the standard negative formula何も…ない).
In everyday speech,なんでも sometimes carries a nuance of exaggeration (“everything …” in a relative sense).
fields.notes:
In spoken language,なんでも can be an exaggeration: “everything …” but understood as “almost everything …”.
At higher levels,なんでも also means “I hear that …” (hearsay), but this is not N5; do not confuse it with the meaning “anything”.
なんでもかんでも is an emphatic form; avoid overusing it in formal written language.
mistakes: Incorrect use with a negative: to say “not eat anything” you must use何も食べない, not “なんでも食べない”.
Confusingなんでもない (it's nothing) with “何でもない= not everything…” → the correct understanding is the set phrase “it's nothing”.
Usingなんでも too broadly leads to exaggeration: consider the context (e.g., “なんでも知っている” is an exaggeration).
In questions about a specific choice, use どれでも/どのNでも instead of なんでも.

rows: Set phrase, not the ordinary “なんでも + ない” structure
<ruby>大丈夫<rt>だいじょうぶ</rt></ruby>、なんでもないよ
どれでも／どこでも／いつでも／だれでも

fields.connection: なんで + [question] (reason; 何で is also used to ask about means: バスで…)
examples: How do you get to school? — I go by bus.
How did you come here today? — I came by bicycle.
How do you get to Tokyo? — I go by train.
fields.explain:
To ask for a reason in casual conversation: use なんで +普通形(plain form).
To be more polite: なんで～んですか, or switch to どうして/なぜ.
To ask about means: なんで + V; the answer is usually N + で.
Use rising intonation at the end of the sentence to show it is a question.

なんで(何で) has 2 main meanings at N5:
Why (casual, everyday conversation). Add ～んですか to be polite: なんで～んですか。
By what (means/method): asks about transportation, tools, etc.
Why (casual, everyday conversation). Add ～んですか to be polite: なんで～んですか。
By what (means/method): asks about transportation, tools, etc.
Tell them apart by looking at the answer:
If the answer uses N + で(バスで, はしで, てで, パソコンで) → it asks about means.
If the answer uses ～から／～ので(雨だから,忙しいので) → it asks about the reason.
If the answer uses N + で(バスで, はしで, てで, パソコンで) → it asks about means.
If the answer uses ～から／～ので(雨だから,忙しいので) → it asks about the reason.
In formal contexts or on exams, prefer どうして/なぜ to ask for a reason; なんで leans toward casual.
fields.notes:
Kanji:何で. Common pronunciation:なんで. When it means “by what”, it can also be understood as “by what means”.
In some contexts, なんで asking for a “reason” can sound blunt; avoid using it with superiors you are not close to.
To ask “how” (a process, step by step) → prefer どうやって to avoid ambiguity.
mistakes: Confusing the meanings: なんで = “by what” or “why”. Use the answer (N+で vs ～から/～ので) to tell them apart.
Using なんで in overly formal contexts → it sounds impolite. Use どうして/なぜ instead.
Wrong pronunciation: writing “なにで” when asking for a reason. The common colloquial standard isなんで; “なにで” mainly means “by what”.

rows: Casual; can be ambiguous without context
Neutral, more polite than なんで
どうして<ruby>来<rt>こ</rt></ruby>ないんですか
なぜ<ruby>遅<rt>おく</rt></ruby>れましたか
どうやって<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きますか

fields.connection: Vます(drop ます)・N(action) + に + 行く・来る・帰る
examples:
I'm going to study Japanese.
I'm going to my Japanese lesson.
fields.explain:
に：Indicates the purpose of an action.

V2 in order to do V1.
V2 is usually a verb of movement such as いきます go, きます come, かえります return, もどります go back…
fields.notes:
For verbal nouns （Nする）：there are 2 ways to use them:
Full sentence: N(place)へ Nを Vに 行きます・来ます・帰ります

examples: I know almost everything about this movie.
Most of the students passed the test.
It hardly rained at all today.
On my days off, I go to the park almost every day.
Yesterday I was at home almost all day.
fields.explain:
Do not add ない when it is already used before a noun: ほとんどのN (not ほとんどのNない).
To emphasize “almost not”, always use it with the negative form: ほとんど～ない／ありません.
With specific quantities, ほとんど emphasizes “almost all”, while だいたい emphasizes “approximately, about”.
In spoken language, “ほとんどは〜” can be used to state the majority of the subject: ほとんどは学生です (most of them are students).

With the affirmative: “almost all/most”. Example: ほとんど分かる = understand almost everything.
With the negative: “hardly” (a very low degree, close to 0). Example: ほとんど分からない.
ほとんどの + N is used to say “most …”. Avoid using “ほとんどN” directly before a noun in standard written language (except in some special cases).
With time/frequency: ほとんど毎日(almost every day), ほとんど一日中(almost all day).
The quantitative nuance is considerably stronger than だいたい (roughly), close to ほぼ (almost completely).
fields.notes:
ほとんど + ありません/ないです is a very common pair at N5; memorize it as a set phrase.
When describing duration: “ほとんど一日中” is more natural than “ほとんど一日” when you mean “all day”.
“ほとんどNだ” can be heard in spoken language: ここはほとんど外国人だ (almost everyone here is a foreigner), but standard written language prefers ほとんどのN.
mistakes: Incorrect use with nouns: × ほとんど学生→ ○ ほとんどの学生(written language). In special cases it may be acceptable in spoken language, but it is not recommended on the exam.
Forgetting the negative when you want to say “hardly”: × ほとんど分かります → ○ ほとんど分かりません.
Confusing it with だいたい: だいたい means “about, roughly” and is not as strong as ほとんど.
Redundant double negative: × ほとんどの人が来ませんない → ○ ほとんどの人が来ません.

rows: ほとんどできる／ほとんどできない
Formal, neutral; close to affirmative ほとんど
ほぼ<ruby>完成<rt>かんせい</rt></ruby>した。
Emphasizes estimation; not as strong as ほとんど
About frequency, not an exact proportion
たいてい<ruby>家<rt>いえ</rt></ruby>で<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べる。
<ruby>全然<rt>ぜんぜん</rt></ruby><ruby>分<rt>わ</rt></ruby>からない。

examples: I can speak Japanese reasonably well.
fields.explain:
Placed before an adjective/verb to indicate an average degree.
In conversation, “まあまあです／まあまあかな” is a safe answer when you don't want to praise or criticize strongly.
The interjection form “まあまあ、…” is used at the beginning of a sentence to ease the mood.
Do not combine it with strong intensifiers such as “とても” or “すごく”.
Politeness: neutral; add です/ます to be polite.

Expresses an average degree: “so-so”, “okay”, “fairly”. Neither very good nor very bad.
Used to be modest or to soften an evaluation, avoiding a strong statement.
As the interjection “まあまあ”, it is used to reassure/calm others: “calm down”.
The nuance depends on the context: mild praise (“pretty good”) or mild criticism (“only so-so”).
fields.notes:
Colloquial phrases: “まあまあかな…”, “まあまあいける” (eating/ drinking/ doing something is okay).
“まあまあの + N”: まあまあの成績(okay grades).
Do not use “とても” + まあまあ (contradictory degrees).
The repeated interjection “まあ、まあ” has a different role; it is usually written in full as “まあまあ”.
mistakes: Using it with strong intensifiers: ×とてもまあまあ → choose one or the other.
Wrong position: ×静かなまあまあ店→ 〇まあまあな静かな店(but the natural way to say it is usually: まあまあ静かな店).
Confusing まだまだ (still a long way to go) with まあまあ (so-so) → the meanings are different.
Overusing it in formal written language: avoid it in academic texts; replace it with “平均的/可もなく不可もない”.

rows: More positive than まあまあ
この<ruby>本<rt>ほん</rt></ruby>はけっこういい。
なかなか<ruby>面白<rt>おもしろ</rt></ruby>い。

examples: It's already night, but he's still awake.
There's still milk in the fridge.
Haven't you finished your homework yet? — No, not yet.
Japanese is still really difficult for me.
fields.explain:
Placed right before the element being emphasized (verb, noun, adjective).
Combines naturally with もう for contrast: もう…／まだ…
“まだです” is a polite short form; the full form is usually “まだVていません”.
“まだまだ” expresses modesty/the expectation that there is still a long way to go.

Indicates a state/activity that is ongoing up to the present: “still”, “yet”.
In questions: expresses an expectation about whether a change has happened yet (“… yet?”).
The short answer “まだです” is equivalent to “not (done) yet”.
“まだまだ” raises the degree: still a long way, still a lot.
fields.notes:
まだ +可能形: まだ行けます (can still go/still have the energy).
まだ +数量: まだ二人来ます (two more people are still coming).
Avoid using まだ with an unsuitable simple past: ×まだ行った → 〇まだ行っていない/まだ行く。
mistakes: Confusing it with もう: “もう起きています” = already up; “まだ起きています” = still awake.
Using “まだ” but forgetting the correct tense: 〇まだしています／×まだします (different meaning: will not do it yet).
Question: “もう食べましたか。” Answer: “まだです。” (correct); ×“まだ。” in formal situations.
“まだに” is not used at N5 (the pattern いまだに is a higher level).

rows: <ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>はまだ<ruby>降<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>っている。
もう<ruby>時間<rt>じかん</rt></ruby>がない。
<ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby>でも<ruby>覚<rt>おぼ</rt></ruby>えている。
